audits.title: Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
audits.genuine_reason: Summary and body lead with a null result: three tools that read model activations did not help predictors beyond reading the transcript. The positive training result is secondary.
experiments: Activation-reading interpretability tools as uplift for predicting counterfactual prompt-edit outcomes
Training models to write open-ended explanations of their own behavior (weaker, mixed; detail only in the paper appendix)
audits.primary_experiment: Activation-reading interpretability tools as uplift for predicting counterfactual prompt-edit outcomes

hypothesis.evidence: Tools were chosen because each helped in earlier auditing games, and the authors call the null surprising, implying they expected uplift.

claim_scope.evidence: Predictor sees transcript, behavior and one proposed edit, plus five read-only activation calls; data from thousands of in-the-wild investigations; authors flag behaviors as simple.

method.evidence: Three activation-reading tools (activation oracles, natural-language autoencoders, sparse autoencoders) versus a transcript-only baseline, scoring probability that a counterfactual prompt edit changes behavior.

models.evidence: Only the predictor, Claude Opus 4.8, is named; the two target models are unnamed, and Gemma appears only in an example.

result_direction.evidence: Predictors using any of the tools scored no better than transcript-only predictors, in every variant tried, including model swaps and hyperparameter sweeps.

failure_type.evidence: Authors report the tools simply did not help, and explain outputs duplicate transcript content and rarely state causal links; result held across hyperparameter sweeps.

quote.value: Our evaluation is a close checkable proxy, and the tools provided no uplift
quote.evidence: Sentence in the discussion section reporting that the evaluated activation tools gave predictors no gain over reading the transcript.

audits.notes: Summary of a longer paper; numeric results are only in figures; target models unnamed for this evaluation.

audits.title: Takeaways from our robust injury classifier project [Redwood Research]
audits.genuine_reason: The post reports an adversarial-training project that missed its goal by a wide margin, plus follow-ups where the classifier still let severe cases through.
experiments: Adversarial training with contractor-written attacks to build an injury classifier with near-zero failures
Follow-up: fitting roughly 6,000 adversarial examples with small classifiers
audits.primary_experiment: Adversarial training with contractor-written attacks to build an injury classifier with near-zero failures

hypothesis.evidence: Goal was a classifier made reliably safe against injurious story completions through adversarial training; the authors say alignment progress fell far below hopes.

claim_scope.evidence: Contractor attacks via rewriting tools on an injury classifier; about 6,000 adversarial examples, small models, one model update; authors say not a clean negative.

method.evidence: Adversarial training on contractor-found failures using attack tools (saliency highlighting, greedy word replacements), checked at a conservative threshold and by random sampling.

models.evidence: Mentions only small models and a classifier; no model names or sizes are given in the post.

result_direction.evidence: Failures remained under random sampling and egregious attacks, though some adversarial robustness gains were measured; outcome was far under the original goal.

failure_type.evidence: Authors say results could stem from suboptimal training choices, such as one model update and borderline training attacks, so the negative is not conclusive.

quote.value: we did not produce a classifier that was actually adversarially robust
quote.evidence: Sentence in the overall-takeaways section stating that no robust classifier resulted from the project.

audits.notes: Authors say this is not a demonstrated negative result; setup details are in the linked paper.

audits.title: Evolutionary prompt optimization for SAE feature visualization
audits.genuine_reason: Leads with a positive method result and most of the body shows working visualizations; the two-feature attempt is one short section plus an appendix.
experiments: Maximizing two SAE features on the same token with a readable prompt
AdvPrompter for maximizing arbitrary features (one sentence only)
audits.primary_experiment: Maximizing two SAE features on the same token with a readable prompt

hypothesis.evidence: No expectation is stated for the two-feature attempt; the post only says the authors tried it.

claim_scope.evidence: One pair of GPT-2 SAE features (layer 10), several combination objectives, very low fluency weight, plus a brief hand-search baseline; run counts not reported.

method.evidence: Evolutionary prompt optimization with fluency penalty; objectives combining both feature activations via sum, min, max or a sub-one Lp norm.

models.evidence: GPT-2 (Small, per the summary) with layer-10 residual SAEs from a named author; Gemma 1 2B is used in other sections.

result_direction.evidence: Both features got high activations only with fluency nearly ignored, below their individual maxima; hand search also failed to co-activate them.

failure_type.evidence: Post says the two features are too distinct to co-activate on one token, but gives no cause fitting any listed category.

quote.value: Both features have high activations, but the activations are not maximum-activating
quote.evidence: Caption under the two-feature results: both features were strongly activated, but short of their individual maxima.

audits.notes: Mostly positive method post; two-feature failure is a short section plus appendix; activation values are in images.

audits.title: Interpreting Preference Models w/ Sparse Autoencoders
audits.genuine_reason: The post is mostly a positive demonstration of features that move reward; ablations that fail to close reward gaps appear in several sections but are secondary.
experiments: Ablating top reward-relevant SAE features to fully close reward gaps (URL, repeated-text, uncertainty-phrase features)
Famous-name and movie features for jailbreak prompts (detail only in a linked comment)
audits.primary_experiment: Ablating top reward-relevant SAE features to fully close reward gaps (URL, repeated-text, uncertainty-phrase features)

hypothesis.evidence: Only a directional expectation is stated (ablating a negative feature raises reward) and it held; no expectation of fully closing gaps appears.

claim_scope.evidence: Six SAEs (layers 2 to 20, 32k features) on one 7B preference model; top 2k of roughly 155k dataset points; custom prompts under 100 tokens.

method.evidence: Gated SAEs on a preference model, attribution patching with integrated gradients to rank features, then single-feature ablation on chosen and custom completions.

models.evidence: Open-source 7B preference model built on GPT-J (6.9B); SAEs are Gated SAEs; checkpoint name is only linked, not written.

result_direction.evidence: Ablation moved reward the expected way, but even the top five URL features, or several repeated-text features, left the gap unclosed.

failure_type.evidence: Post only floats maybes (feature splitting, other unexplained reasons, SAE limits) and never settles on a cause or says it is unclear.

quote.value: We do not explain 100% of reward differences through SAE features
quote.evidence: Takeaway bullet near the top: after a couple of hours of trying, SAE features leave part of the reward difference unexplained.

audits.notes: Mostly positive post; most reward-gap results are in images, not text.

audits.title: Training Model to Predict Its Own Generalization: A Preliminary Study
audits.genuine_reason: Summary leads with early positive results and most of the body reports wins (4B, 14B); the 0.5B result and the failed replication are shorter sections.
experiments: MetaSFT on Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Base predicting emergent-misalignment generalization
Replicating human-unpredictable surprising generalization with models up to 14B for validation
audits.primary_experiment: MetaSFT on Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Base predicting emergent-misalignment generalization

hypothesis.evidence: Authors give reasons to expect the meta-training pipeline to work (existing introspection, learnable behavior modes); the 0.5B run contradicted this.

claim_scope.evidence: 100 advice domains split 50 and 50, 2,500 training domain pairs, three held-out quadrants; LLM-judge evilness score with RMSE; one 0.5B base model.

method.evidence: Meta-training the model on ICL-versus-SFT outcome pairs, compared with ground-truth fine-tuning baselines, untrained in-context learning, and correlation after calibration adjustment.

models.evidence: Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Base for the failed run; Qwen-3-4B-Base for the positive contrast run.

result_direction.evidence: MetaSFT lost to ground-truth baselines on RMSE because of miscalibration; on correlation it beat one baseline but not the other, a weak outcome.

failure_type.evidence: Post cites miscalibration and a degenerate evaluation where training barely matters, but gives no root cause mapping to a listed category.

quote.value: Results are negative for the former (0.5B) but positive for the latter (4B)
quote.evidence: Sentence in the emergent-misalignment section giving the outcome by model size: failure at the smaller model, success at the larger.

audits.notes: Mostly positive preliminary study; 0.5B result and failed replication are brief; numbers are in figures.

audits.title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior
audits.genuine_reason: Summary leads with positive held-out generalization and most of the body covers it; the weaker open-ended results and the privileged-access null are real but secondary sections.
experiments: Privileged-access test: training a subject model versus a different 8B model on the same behavior data
Open-ended self-explanation training generalizing to the hint setting
Self-explanations as aids for counterfactual simulators (help weak, hurt strong)
audits.primary_experiment: Privileged-access test: training a subject model versus a different 8B model on the same behavior data

hypothesis.evidence: A model with introspective access should beat a cross-trained one on its own behavior; one author had guessed some privileged access would show.

claim_scope.evidence: Self and cross training of two 8B models on counterfactual claim data from in-the-wild investigations, evaluated on held-out claims; claim counts not stated.

method.evidence: Standard privileged-access design: train the subject and a different model on the subject's claims, compare predictors against an Opus transcript-reading reference.

models.evidence: Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as subjects, with Opus 4.8 as the transcript-reading reference.

result_direction.evidence: A model trained on another model's data predicted the subject as well as the subject trained on itself, in both directions.

failure_type.evidence: Relies on the closing discussion: authors read the null as consistent with a prior null and conclude training struggles to surface self-only information.

quote.value: We find no privileged access for our self-explanations
quote.evidence: Opening sentence of the privileged-access results paragraph, reporting that training gave the subject model no self-advantage.

audits.notes: Authors are uncertain why a prior study found privileged access with the same models; follow-up to the evaluation post.
